analysis.one_liner: Redefines who counts as an employee under federal wage-and-hour law, using a narrower test that makes more workers independent contractors.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote in the House Education and Labor Committee and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change how the Fair Labor Standards Act decides who counts as an "employee," using the narrower common-law test, which turns mainly on how much control the employer has over the work. That would replace the law's broader standard, under which workers can be covered even without tight control. The practical effect would be that more workers — particularly gig drivers and delivery workers — could be treated as independent contractors, who are not entitled to the federal minimum wage, overtime, or other wage-and-hour protections.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers that benefit from treating workers as independent contractors would gain: gig-economy platforms, franchisors, staffing agencies, and delivery and rideshare companies. A common-law control test is narrower than the current Fair Labor Standards Act standard, so more workers could be kept off payroll for minimum wage and overtime purposes, and businesses would face less exposure to misclassification lawsuits and wage-and-hour enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gig platforms, franchisors, and staffing firms

how_it_helps.text: It gives employers a single, predictable classification standard by writing the common-law control test into the FLSA itself, replacing what supporters describe as an inconsistent multi-factor approach.
It preserves workers' ability to be treated as independent contractors, which supporters argue protects flexible and entrepreneurial work arrangements.

analysis.who_pays: Workers who would be reclassified as independent contractors would lose Fair Labor Standards Act protections: the federal minimum wage, overtime pay, and coverage for hours worked. They would also lose access to the remedies (back wages, liquidated damages) that come with employee status, with no replacement benefits offered in the bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gig workers and other misclassified employees

drawbacks.text: The common-law test turns on employer control, which is narrower than the FLSA's current standard; it would make it easier to classify workers as independent contractors and take them outside minimum wage and overtime protections.
Workers moved to contractor status would lose federal wage-and-hour coverage with no substitute benefits, paid time, or safety net offered in the bill.
It would create a mismatch between the FLSA definition and other laws, since the bill does not touch the definitions used by the IRS, the National Labor Relations Act, or state laws.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a clearer classification rule for businesses — is real but modest, and the bill does not address the overlap with other definitions of employee. The cost falls entirely on workers: a narrower employee test under the FLSA means fewer people guaranteed the minimum wage, overtime, and back-pay remedies, in a period when courts and agencies were already debating exactly how broad the current standard is. On balance, the bill's design transfers wage protections to employer discretion without giving workers anything in return.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote until the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor on the day it was introduced and received no further action for the rest of the 117th Congress.
It never reached a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, so the current broader FLSA definition of employee remained law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers who would have been reclassified under the narrower test are better off because the bill died, since the broader federal employee test stayed in place. No employer gained anything from the bill's end.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; workers simply kept the existing test

for.name: Rep. Elise Stefanik
for.role: House sponsor, chair of the House Republican Conference
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to apply the common-law control test to the FLSA definition of employee.

for.name: 8 House Republican cosponsors (Reps. Steel, Norman, Gaetz, Cole, Miller, Rodgers, Hern and one more)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat signed on; the Democratic-controlled House Education and Labor Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: App-based delivery and rideshare companies rely on classifying drivers as independent contractors. A narrower common-law test would reduce the risk that drivers are found to be employees entitled to minimum wage and overtime, shifting labor costs from the platforms to the workers.

Franchisors and staffing firms are frequent targets of joint-employer and misclassification claims. The common-law control standard would narrow who counts as an employee, cutting their wage-and-hour liability.

The bill changes the definition of employee across all FLSA coverage, so any employer that currently treats workers as contractors would face a lower risk of reclassification. Large employers that already classify correctly would see little change.
